Search is degraded right now. Queries are slow, timing out, or coming back with partial results. The rest of the product is fine.

What to tell customers: we know, we're working on it, and nothing is lost. Data is intact, and results will be complete again once search recovers. If someone can't find a record, it exists, it just isn't indexed at the moment.

No ETA yet. I'll post an update here every 30 minutes whether or not there's news, and the all-clear will land in this channel first.

Status page: `<status-page-url>`. If a customer reports something that looks unrelated to search, flag it here rather than assuming it's part of this.

I don't know what your 4.0 upgrade actually touched, so the body below is plausible, not real. Keep the shape, swap the specifics for what you changed.

```
Upgrade Postgres driver 3.1 -> 4.0

4.0 removes the implicit connection pool that 3.x created on first query.
Pools are now constructed explicitly, so `db/connect.go` builds one at
startup and passes it through instead of relying on driver internals.

Also renamed the timeout settings to the 4.0 names (`connect_timeout` ->
`ConnectTimeout`, `statement_timeout` -> `StatementTimeout`) and dropped
the retry wrapper in `db/retry.go`, which 4.0 handles natively.

Unit and integration suites pass against Postgres 15. Not yet exercised
against 13, which is still what staging runs.
```

The last line is the one worth keeping in whatever form is true for you. A commit that says which version it was tested against saves the next person a bisect.

Two takes. They differ in how close you are to the person.

**Close colleague:**
Thanks for taking my pages this weekend. I owe you one, and I mean the real kind, not the kind people say.

**Someone you work with less often:**
Thank you for covering my on-call shift last week, it made a genuinely hard week easier. Tell me when you want one back and it's yours.

I'd send the second unless you two already talk like the first. It travels better and still commits you to something.

Two takes, depending on how much room the tooltip has.

**Full:**
Archive removes this project from your active list and makes it read-only. Nothing is deleted. You can restore it anytime from Settings > Archived.

**Tight (under ~60 chars of hover space):**
Hides the project and makes it read-only. Nothing is deleted.

I'd ship the full one. The whole reason people hesitate on Archive is that they can't tell it apart from Delete, and the restore path is what settles that.

One thing to check before it ships: I assumed archiving is fully reversible and doesn't stop anything running. If it cancels scheduled jobs, revokes collaborator access, or changes billing, that belongs in the tooltip and neither take says it.

Thirty minutes only works here if the options are written down before the meeting, so the pre-read is part of the agenda, not a nicety.

**Decide: mobile release cadence** (30 min)

**Owner:** `<name>`. **Decider:** `<name>`. If the decider can't be in the room, move the meeting.

**Pre-read (sent 24h ahead, 1 page):** current cadence, last quarter's actual ship dates, time spent per release on cut/QA/store review, and the two or three candidate cadences with their tradeoffs.

1. **Where we are now** (5 min). What we actually shipped last quarter versus what we planned, and what the release overhead costs per cycle. Facts only, no proposals.
2. **What's forcing the change** (5 min). Store review latency, hotfix frequency, QA capacity, whatever is actually hurting. If nothing is hurting, we end the meeting here.
3. **Options on the table** (10 min). Weekly, biweekly, monthly train, each with what it demands of QA and release engineering. Five minutes for questions, not for relitigating the pre-read.
4. **Decide** (7 min). Decider picks. If we can't pick, we name the one missing fact and who gets it by when, and that is the outcome.
5. **First consequences** (3 min). Who owns the release train, what changes in the branch cut, when the new cadence starts.

**Out of scope, say so out loud if it comes up:** feature flag strategy, the CI backlog, and whether Android and iOS ship together. That last one is a real question and probably needs its own 30 minutes.

Two things I'd change with more context: whether Android and iOS genuinely have to share a cadence, and whether there's a decider at all or this is a group that needs consensus. If it's consensus, 30 minutes isn't enough and I'd say so before booking it.

Two notes before you send. The specifics in the third paragraph have to be real; a generic "close call" line reads worse than no line at all, and candidates compare notes. And only offer the feedback call if you'll actually take it, since an unanswered reply to that offer is the part people remember.

Repo name, command name, and the connection string convention are placeholders. Everything else holds for a seeder of this shape.

```markdown
# seedy

Seeds a local or staging database with realistic test data.

`seedy` exists so you don't have to click through signup six times to
reproduce a bug. It creates accounts, projects, and activity history that
look like a real workspace: varied dates, mixed states, some records
deliberately broken so error paths get exercised.

## Quick start

    go install ./cmd/seedy
    export DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost:5432/app_dev
    seedy small

That gives you 3 accounts, 12 projects, and ~200 events, in about four
seconds. Run `seedy --help` for the other sizes.

## What it does to your database

`seedy` truncates every table it seeds before inserting. It does not ask
first. It refuses to run against a `DATABASE_URL` whose host is not
`localhost` unless you pass `--i-know`, which is the only guardrail
between you and a very bad afternoon.

It does not run migrations. Bring your own schema.
```

The "what it does to your database" section is the one I'd fight to keep. A seeder that truncates is the single fact a new person needs before they run it, and it belongs above the flag reference, not in it.

Two assumptions worth checking: that yours truncates rather than appends, and that the host guard exists. If it doesn't guard on host, that paragraph is a feature request rather than documentation.

One line above the paragraph, because leadership will ask and you want the answer in the same message: this says we're late, why, and when we'll know more. It does not ask for anything, so add an ask if you have one.

The database migration is running about two weeks behind the original date, and we now expect to complete cutover in the week of `<date>` rather than `<original date>`. The delay came from the backfill: two of the largest tables have foreign key relationships we hadn't accounted for, which forced a serialized backfill instead of the parallel one we planned, and that costs roughly nine days of machine time we can't compress. The work itself is on track and nothing has been descoped; four of six services are already reading from the new database in production without incident. The remaining risk is the cutover window for the last two services, which is the only step that requires downtime, and we'll know by `<date>` whether that fits in the maintenance window we've already booked. If it doesn't, the fallback is a second window two weeks later, and I'll flag that as soon as we know rather than at the deadline.

The dates and the table specifics are mine and need replacing with yours. The structure is the part I'd keep: new date first, cause second, what's already working third, remaining risk last with a date attached to it. A status update without a date on the next checkpoint invites a follow-up meeting.

Make it reproducible before you make it fixed. One in five means you can get a failure in ten runs, which is cheap, and almost everything else you'd try is guesswork until you can trigger it on demand.

1. **Get the data.** Run the suite in a loop, 50 times, and record which tests failed each time. `for i in $(seq 50); do <test-cmd> --seed=$i; done` into a log you can count. You're looking for whether it's one test, a cluster, or genuinely scattered.
2. **Read what the distribution tells you.** One test failing 20% of the time is a bug in that test. Twenty different tests each failing rarely is shared state or ordering, and you should stop looking at individual tests. Failures clustered at the end of a run point at resource exhaustion: connections, file handles, memory.
3. **Attack ordering first if it's scattered.** Most runners can randomize and then replay a seed. Find a seed that fails, then bisect the test list under that seed until you have the minimal pair: test A passes alone, fails after test B. That pair names the shared state.
4. **Check the usual four.** Time (tests that assume "now" or a timezone, and break near midnight or a DST boundary), ordering (leaked global state, a database row not rolled back), concurrency (a real race, or a test that waits a fixed 100ms for something async), and external dependencies (a network call, a container that isn't ready yet).
5. **Quarantine, don't delete.** Move confirmed flakes to a separately-tracked job so the main suite goes green and stays trusted. Put a deadline on the quarantine list or it becomes permanent.

**The one thing I'd push back on:** a fixed `sleep` in a test is a flake with a longer fuse, not a fix. If you find yourself lengthening one, that test is telling you something is actually racy in the code under test, and that race is probably in production too.

**Bet on where it is:** shared database state between tests, if you're on a suite with real database access and a transaction rollback strategy that has any exceptions to it. That's the most common one by a wide margin at this failure rate.

Fix CI. Splitting the monorepo at 40 engineers trades a 30-minute build for permanent cross-repo version coordination, and that second cost never goes away.

**Why the split is worse than it looks.** Splitting doesn't remove work, it relocates it. You get faster individual builds and, in exchange, versioned internal dependencies, changes that now span three PRs in three repos, and the day someone ships a breaking change to a library that four teams pin at different versions. At 40 engineers you'll feel that within a quarter. Companies that split successfully mostly do it at a scale where team boundaries are already hard, and they staff a platform team to absorb the coordination cost.

**Thirty minutes is almost never irreducible.** Before accepting it as a constraint, get the breakdown: how much is install and setup versus actual test execution, how much runs on every PR that didn't touch the affected code, and how much is one slow serialized stage everyone waits behind.

**Three things to try, in order of return per hour spent:**

1. **Affected-only builds.** Turn on task-level caching and dependency-graph-based selection, whatever your build system offers. This is usually the single biggest win, because most PRs touch a small fraction of the graph. Nx, Bazel, Turborepo, or your build tool's equivalent.
2. **Remote caching.** A build someone already ran shouldn't run again. Frequently cuts CI time more than parallelism does, and costs less.
3. **Bigger and more parallel runners.** The least elegant option and often the fastest to land. Engineer time at 40 people is worth vastly more than CI machines. If you can buy 30 minutes down to 12 for a few thousand a year, do that this week while the other two land.

**Where I'd be wrong.** If the 30 minutes is genuinely a single serialized integration test suite that can't be split, or the pain is really about ownership and review bottlenecks rather than clock time, then the problem isn't CI and neither is the answer. Splitting still wouldn't fix it, but you'd be solving the wrong thing either way.

**Your call, not mine, on one thing:** whether the pressure to split is technical or organizational. If a director wants their own repo for reasons that aren't build times, the CI work won't end the conversation.

Idempotent means calling it twice does the same thing as calling it once. That's the whole definition; the interesting part is why you need it.

**Where it bites you.** A client sends `POST /charges` for $50. The request reaches your server, you charge the card, and then the connection drops before the response gets back. The client sees a timeout. It has no way to know whether the charge happened, so it retries. Now the customer paid $100.

The client did nothing wrong. Retrying a request that timed out is correct behavior, and every HTTP library, mobile app on a bad connection, and message queue you'll ever use does it. So the server has to be the one that can absorb a duplicate.

**What you already have that's idempotent.** In your CRUD endpoints, `GET`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` are naturally idempotent. `GET /users/5` twice returns the same user. `PUT /users/5` with a full body sets those fields to those values, and doing it twice leaves the same row. `DELETE /users/5` deletes the user, and the second call finds nothing to delete, which is fine.

`POST` is the one that isn't, because "create a new thing" means a second call creates a second thing. That's also why almost every payment API you've seen makes you pass an idempotency key.

**How to make POST idempotent.** The client generates a unique key, usually a UUID, and sends it as a header: `Idempotency-Key: 7f3e...`. On the server:

1. Look up the key in a table before doing any work.
2. If it exists, return the stored response from the first call. Don't do the work again.
3. If it doesn't, do the work and store the key with the response, in the same transaction as the work itself.

That last clause is the part people get wrong. If you charge the card and then write the key in a separate step, a crash in between puts you right back where you started.

**One trap.** "Retry-safe" is not the same as "unchanged." A `PUT` that sets `updated_at = now()` is still idempotent in the way that matters, since the resource ends in the same state, but a `PUT` that increments a counter is not, and neither is one that appends to a list. When you're deciding whether something is idempotent, ask about the state it leaves behind, not whether every byte in the database is identical.

Hire the senior generalist, unless you already have someone with real slack in their week who wants to mentor. That condition is the whole decision, and most teams that think they have it don't.

**Two juniors are a bet on your capacity, not on them.** Two juniors cost roughly one senior in salary and roughly one senior in attention. The mentoring load is real: code review, unblocking, pairing, direction-setting, and it comes out of whoever on your team is already most in demand. For the first six to nine months, two juniors typically produce less than zero net output, because they consume more senior time than they generate. That's not a knock on juniors, it's just what the ramp costs, and it's a cost people forget to price.

**When each one wins:**

| | Senior generalist | Two juniors |
|---|---|---|
| **Time to net-positive** | Weeks | 6-12 months |
| **Requires from you** | Clear problems, autonomy | Sustained mentoring capacity |
| **Best when** | Team is stretched, work is ambiguous, no one has slack | Team is stable, work is well-defined, someone actively wants to grow people |
| **Main risk** | One person, one point of failure, may leave in 2 years | Ramp cost lands on your best engineer |
| **Longer-term upside** | Immediate leverage | Two people who know your system deeply and cost less |

**The question that actually decides it:** name the specific person who will mentor them, and go ask if they want to. Not "the team will help." A name. If nobody says yes with enthusiasm, hire the senior, because juniors without a real mentor churn out or plateau, and that outcome is worse for them than not being hired.

**One caveat I wouldn't compress away.** "Senior generalist" is the easiest role to hire badly, because the bar is fuzzy and interviewers reward breadth of vocabulary. Write down the three problems you want them solving in their first six months before you open the req. If you can't, you probably want a specialist and haven't admitted it yet.

Give them a number, but make it four numbers and one sentence, and start by finding out what they're actually going to do with it. Refusing outright loses the argument and gets you a worse metric picked without you.

**Ask the real question first.** "Single number for productivity" is usually a proxy for something specific: are we investing enough in engineering, is a particular team stuck, why did the last three things ship late, or can I defend headcount to the board. Each of those has a different answer, and most of them aren't a productivity number at all. Get this in a one-on-one before the deck exists, because once a number is in a board deck it never leaves.

**What to offer instead.** The DORA four are the least-bad standard answer, and they have the advantage of being an industry standard you didn't invent:

- **Deployment frequency.** How often we ship to production.
- **Lead time for changes.** Commit to running in production.
- **Change failure rate.** What fraction of deploys cause a problem.
- **Time to restore.** How long to recover when one does.

They measure the system, not the people, which is the property that keeps them from being gamed into uselessness. Pair them with one sentence of narrative each month explaining what moved and why. The sentence is not decoration, it's the thing that stops a two-point dip from becoming a meeting.

**Say this part out loud, early.** Any single number gets optimized the moment it's tied to evaluation. Lines of code gives you copy-paste. Story points gives you inflation, and you'll get it within a quarter, reliably. Tickets closed gives you split tickets. This isn't a hypothetical risk and leadership generally understands Goodhart's law when it's named plainly, they just haven't connected it to this request.

**If they insist on exactly one:** give them deployment frequency, or lead time. Both are hard to fake without actually getting better, and both are visibly a team property rather than an individual one. Never per-engineer, never in a performance review. That's the line I'd hold even if you concede the rest.

**Your call:** whether to push back in the room or bring the alternative to the next one. If the request came with a deadline attached, bring the DORA four as the answer rather than as a counterproposal. Framing it as compliance rather than negotiation gets it adopted.

Get tests around it before you change a line. The fear is rational, since nobody knows what the module does, and the only thing that converts fear into safety is a suite that fails when you break something.

**The order matters more than the technique:**

1. **Find out what it actually does in production.** Add logging or tracing at its boundaries and let it run for a week. You'll learn which paths are hot, which are dead, and which callers exist that nobody remembered. Dead code you can delete is the cheapest win available and it usually shrinks the problem meaningfully.
2. **Write characterization tests, not correct tests.** Feed it real inputs, capture whatever it returns, and assert that. Including the wrong behavior. You are not documenting what it should do, you're pinning what it does, so you'll notice if a refactor changes it. Golden-file tests are perfect for this and take an afternoon.
3. **Seal the boundary.** Give it a narrow interface and route every caller through that. `grep` for every call site, including reflection and string-built names if the language allows them. Once the surface is small and known, the inside becomes yours to change.
4. **Change the inside in small, individually shippable pieces.** Extract one function, ship it, wait. The temptation is a two-week rewrite branch, and that branch is how these efforts die: it drifts from main, the person on it gets pulled away, and six weeks later it's abandoned.
5. **Delete the scaffolding when you're done.** The characterization tests that pinned wrong behavior should be replaced by tests that assert right behavior, once you know what right is.

**Where the real danger is,** and it isn't in the module: it's in the callers you didn't find. Before you touch the shared function, enumerate every call site. A guard added inside the shared function is a smaller and safer change than a guard added in each caller, and it's the version that fixes the paths nobody filed a ticket about.

**The thing that makes this stick.** Pick one person to own it, and give them a real allocation, not "as time allows." Scary modules stay scary because everyone touching them is doing it in the margins of something else, and margin work doesn't produce the sustained attention this needs. Two focused weeks beats four months of Fridays.

**One I'd skip:** don't rewrite it from scratch. You'll rediscover every edge case the original handled, one production incident at a time, and the ones you'll rediscover last are the rare ones that mattered most.

A preflight failure means the browser asked your server for permission before sending the real request, and your server didn't grant it. Your actual request never ran. Nothing hit your handler.

**What's happening mechanically.** For requests that aren't "simple" (anything using `PUT`, `DELETE`, `PATCH`, a custom header like `Authorization` or `X-Api-Key`, or a `Content-Type` of `application/json`), the browser first sends an `OPTIONS` request to the same URL, carrying:

```
Origin: https://app.example.com
Access-Control-Request-Method: POST
Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type, authorization
```

Your server has to answer that `OPTIONS` with `200` or `204` and headers that explicitly permit each of those things:

```
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: POST
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: content-type, authorization
```

If any of those is missing or doesn't cover what was asked, the browser blocks the real request and logs a CORS error. The block happens in the browser, on the response, which is why the error message is vague: the browser deliberately doesn't tell JavaScript much about a response it isn't allowed to read.

**The three causes, in order of how often they're it:**

1. **Your framework doesn't route `OPTIONS`.** You defined a `POST` handler for `/api/thing` and nothing answers `OPTIONS /api/thing`, so it 404s and the browser calls that a failure. Extremely common.
2. **A header isn't in `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`.** You allowed `content-type` and the client also sends `authorization`, or a tracing header your SDK adds without telling you. The list must cover every header the browser named, and it isn't a wildcard when credentials are involved.
3. **Credentials.** If the request sends cookies, `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` is invalid. You must echo the exact origin and also send `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`.

**How to see the actual answer** rather than guessing: open the network tab, find the `OPTIONS` request, not the one that failed, and read its response headers. The browser console error is close to useless; the `OPTIONS` response tells you exactly which permission is missing. Or from the shell:

```
curl -i -X OPTIONS https://api.example.com/thing \
  -H 'Origin: https://app.example.com' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: POST' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type, authorization'
```

**The caveat worth keeping.** CORS is not a server-side security control. It restricts what browser JavaScript can read from another origin, and that's all. It does nothing about `curl`, a mobile app, or a server-to-server call, so setting `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on an endpoint that returns private data doesn't create the leak, it just removes the browser's objection to one that's already there. Authentication is a separate job and CORS never does it for you.

Look at what's shared. A gap that big between p50 and p99 almost always means contention on something every request touches, not slow code, because slow code makes p50 slow too.

**Get the shape of it before you tune anything.** Four questions, and the answers point at completely different fixes:

- **Is the p99 the same endpoints as the p50, or a different set?** Different endpoints means you don't have a latency problem, you have three slow routes dragging the aggregate, and you should stop reading percentiles across all traffic.
- **Is it the same users every time?** Same accounts consistently slow means data skew: one tenant with 100x the rows, a query that's fine at 1,000 records and quadratic at 100,000.
- **Is it bursty or steady?** Latency that spikes at intervals is a background job, a cache expiry stampede, or GC. Steady p99 is queueing.
- **Where does the time go inside one slow request?** If you have distributed tracing, pull a single p99 trace and look at the span breakdown. This one question often ends the investigation, and everything below is what to do when you don't have tracing.

**The four usual causes, ranked by how often they're it at this ratio:**

1. **Connection pool exhaustion.** The most common by a distance. Your pool holds 20 connections; at peak, request 21 waits. The waiting shows up as latency with no slow query in the database logs, which is exactly why it's hard to find. Check pool wait time as a metric, not pool size.
2. **A query with no index on a tail case.** A query that's fast for typical row counts and terrible for your largest accounts. `pg_stat_statements` or the equivalent, sorted by max time rather than mean, since mean hides precisely this.
3. **Queueing under load.** If your service is near capacity, small bursts produce large tail latency, and it's nonlinear: at 80% utilization the tail is fine, at 95% it's catastrophic. Look at CPU utilization at peak, not average. Averages over a minute hide a five-second pileup completely.
4. **A downstream call without a timeout.** One dependency occasionally takes 4 seconds and you wait for it. 4 seconds exactly is a suspicious number, that's a default timeout or a retry pattern somewhere. Worth checking early on the strength of the number alone.

**What I'd do first,** concretely: add a metric for connection pool wait time, and pull one p99 trace end to end. Between those two you'll usually know within a day, and neither requires changing any behavior.

**One thing not to do yet.** Don't add caching. It'll move p50 down, make the dashboard look better, and leave the tail exactly where it is, because the requests that miss the cache are the same ones that were already slow. Fix the cause, then cache if you still want the p50.
